title: Your First Project Folder and Safe Working Habits
learningObjectives: Explain what a project folder is and why all files belonging to one website should be kept inside a clearly named root folder.
Create a simple project structure with a main page and separate folders for stylesheets, scripts and images, choosing folders that fit the project's size.
Describe the purpose of common files such as index.html, styles.css and app.js, and explain why a clear entry page helps people find the project starting point.
Choose descriptive, consistent file and folder names that communicate purpose, avoid confusing variations and make the project easier to maintain.
Distinguish an absolute path from a relative path and check that links between HTML, CSS, JavaScript and image files point to the correct locations.
Create, save, reopen and test a project file, and explain why saving changes regularly prevents accidental loss of work.
Describe the difference between a backup and version history, and choose a suitable basic method to recover an earlier copy after an unwanted change.
Use a small-step workflow: make one change, save it, refresh or retest the page, observe the result and investigate an error before making another change.
Identify sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, private keys, access tokens and personal data, and explain why they must not be placed in public website files or client-side code.
Explain that files delivered to a browser can be inspected by users, and identify safer places such as server-side secret storage for credentials that must remain private.
Check whether images, fonts, code snippets and other third-party assets may legally be reused, and keep attribution or licence information when required.
Prepare a small project handover by keeping its folders understandable, removing unnecessary temporary files, documenting how to open it and preserving a recoverable copy.

understand.concept: A project folder is the clearly named root location that keeps the files for one website or small application together. A beginner project might place its main page at the root and group supporting files into folders such as `css/`, `js/` and `images/`. This is a useful starting arrangement, not a universal rule; the structure should grow only when the project needs it. Use names that describe each file's purpose and keep the naming style consistent.
understand.whyItMatters: A predictable project structure makes work easier to find, review, test, share and hand over. Safe working habits matter just as much: save work regularly, keep a recoverable copy, check permissions before reusing third-party assets, and never place credentials or private data in files that are delivered to a browser.
understand.history: This lesson focuses on practical project organization and safe working habits used in current web development.
understand.analogy: Think of a project folder as a workshop with labelled storage areas. The labels help you find the right tool or material without searching through everything.
understand.analogyLimit: Real projects do not all need the same layout. Frameworks, build tools, team conventions and project size can change the structure. A backup is also different from version control, which records a sequence of changes.

explain.narrative:
Build a small project in a deliberate order. First create a root folder named `my-first-site/`. Add `index.html` as the page you will open, then create `css/`, `js/` and `images/` folders. Put `styles.css`, `app.js` and `logo.png` in their matching folders. In `index.html`, reference the stylesheet with `href="css/styles.css"` and the script with `src="js/app.js"`. The path must match the actual names and locations exactly.

Next, open the page and check that its resources load. If the styling is missing, verify the stylesheet reference and confirm that the file exists at that location. If an image or script is missing, check its corresponding path. Save after each meaningful change and test again so that a mistake is easy to locate.

Protect the project as you work. Keep a backup outside the working folder or use version control so you can recover an earlier state. Remember that HTML, CSS and JavaScript sent to a browser can be inspected by visitors; do not put passwords, private keys, access tokens or private API credentials there. Store secrets in an appropriate server-side environment. Before copying an image, font or code sample, check its licence and any attribution requirements.

examples.code:
my-first-site/
  index.html
  css/
    styles.css
  js/
    app.js
  images/
    logo.png

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">
<script src="js/app.js" defer></script>
examples.explanation: This structure keeps the entry page, styles, scripts and images in predictable locations. The relative paths connect the HTML page to the matching files.
examples.expectedOutput: A small website project with a clear root folder, separate subfolders and matching file paths.

practise.guidedTask: Create a `my-first-site` folder on your computer. Inside it, create `index.html`, `css/styles.css`, `js/app.js` and an `images/` folder. Add the CSS and JavaScript paths to the HTML file. Add a heading, open the page in a browser, and check that the stylesheet and script load. Save after each change.
practise.independentTask: Design a folder structure for a small personal profile website. List the HTML, CSS, JavaScript and image files it needs. Identify which files will be public and which information must remain secret. Explain how you will keep a backup or version history. Write brief instructions so another person can open the project.
hints: Start with one clearly named root folder and keep the project files inside it.
Use a consistent naming convention; names should explain each file's purpose.
Check that relative paths in HTML match the real folder structure.
Save and test after each important change.
Never place passwords, API keys, private keys or access tokens in public files.
Use backups and version control; they are related but not identical.
Check licences or permissions before reusing images, fonts or code.

questions.prompt: What is the most reliable way to organize a small website project?
options: Leave all files randomly on the desktop
Use a clearly named root folder and meaningful subfolders
Give every file the same name
questions.answer: Use a clearly named root folder and meaningful subfolders
questions.explanation: A root folder and clear subfolders make files, paths and project handover easier to manage.

questions.prompt: What should never be placed in a public JavaScript file delivered to a browser?
options: A private API key or password
questions.answer: A private API key or password
questions.explanation: Users can inspect code delivered to their browser. Keep secrets in server-side secret storage.

questions.prompt: If a CSS file does not load, what should you check first?
options: The stylesheet path and file name in the HTML
questions.answer: The stylesheet path and file name in the HTML
questions.explanation: A wrong relative path or file name can stop the browser from finding the stylesheet.

questions.prompt: Why are backups and version history useful?
options: They remove the need to test code
They help recover earlier work after an unwanted change or loss
They remove the need for a project folder
questions.answer: They help recover earlier work after an unwanted change or loss
questions.explanation: A backup keeps an extra copy; version control records changes and can help restore an earlier state.
